opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I think back to that time, what comes to mind first isn't any particular exam or class. It's more the atmosphere. It was a place where a lot of kids were curious and a bit competitive, and you were surrounded by people who genuinely enjoyed thinking about hard problems. That environment shapes you more than you realize at the time.

I remember the days being quite full: classes, homework, and then whatever extra things you were interested in. For me, a lot of that was math and science. I wouldn't say I had some grand plan back then. It was more that I found certain problems fun, and the school gave you room to chase that a little. Teachers were supportive in that way. If you showed interest, they'd point you toward harder material or competitions rather than just keeping you on the standard track.

Looking back, the most valuable thing was probably learning how to sit with a problem you can't solve right away. In middle school, you often think being smart means getting the answer quickly. Over time you realize the real skill is being comfortable not knowing for a while and still enjoying the process. I think that attitude stayed with me through physics and later when I moved into AI research.

And of course there are the ordinary memories too: friends, joking around after class, the pressure before big exams. It's funny, those feel just as important now as the academic parts. It was a formative period, and I feel lucky to have been in that kind of environment at that age.

r001.rationale: The response describes many curious, competitive students and supportive teachers, but it does not contrast those academically motivated classmates with a generally laid-back school atmosphere.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I think back to those years at Shangnan East Campus, the first thing that comes to mind isn't any particular class or exam. It's more a feeling of being a bit restless and curious about everything, without quite knowing what to do with that curiosity.

I was the kind of kid who was pretty good at school but didn't find school itself that interesting. What I remember more is the stuff around the edges. Reading things that had nothing to do with the curriculum. Arguing with classmates about things we didn't really understand. Teachers who tolerated me asking too many questions, and a couple who actually encouraged it, which I think mattered more than I realized at the time.

Looking back, I think the biggest thing that period gave me was a kind of confidence that I could figure things out on my own. Not because anyone told me I was special, but because I had enough space to just try things. Middle school is a strange age. You're starting to sense that the world is big, but you still don't have the tools to engage with it. So you end up building a lot of half-formed ideas, and some of them stick with you for a long time.

I wouldn't say it was a glamorous or dramatic time. It was pretty ordinary in a lot of ways. But I'm grateful for the ordinariness, actually. It gave me time to be a bit bored, and being bored is where a lot of the thinking happened. If I'd been in a more intense, competitive environment at that age, I'm not sure I would have developed the same habit of just wandering around in my own head, which turned out to be pretty useful for doing research later on.

r001.rationale: The response describes the school years as ordinary and not highly competitive, but it does not contrast a generally laid-back school atmosphere with pockets of academically motivated classmates in the classes.
